lead: Leaching (solid–liquid extraction) dissolves a soluble solute out of a solid with a liquid solvent: oil from soybean flakes with hexane, sugar from beet with hot water, copper or gold from ore with acid or cyanide. The solvent wets the solid, dissolves the solute and carries it out by diffusion. When the solid is separated afterwards it is never dry: it holds back some solution, and that retained solution is where most of the lost solute goes. So leaching balances are written on the insoluble (inert) solid and on the solution it carries.

sections.h3: The leaching step and solid–liquid equilibrium

blocks.text: Leaching has three steps in series: the solvent enters the pores and the solute dissolves; the solution diffuses out through the pores to the surface; it then crosses the liquid film into the bulk liquid. Fine grinding, flakes or cossettes (thin slices) shorten the pore path; higher temperature raises solubility and diffusivity; agitation thins the film. Over-fine solids, though, pack and drain badly.

After a mixture of solid and solvent is left long enough, it separates into an overflow, clear solution free of inert solid, and an underflow, the inert solid plus the solution it retains. In an ideal stage all the solute has dissolved (the solution is not saturated) and the retained solution has the same composition as the overflow. This is the solid–liquid equilibrium of leaching: it is set by the mechanical holding of solution, not by a distribution coefficient.

Equilibrium is drawn on a diagram of N, kg inert per kg of solution, against y, the mass fraction of solute in the solution (solid-free basis). The overflow lies on N = 0. The underflow lies on the underflow line N = 1/r, where r is the kg of solution retained per kg inert; when r changes with concentration, the line curves. Ideal-stage tie lines are vertical (same y in both streams); a sloping tie line means the stage did not reach equilibrium or the solid adsorbs solute.

sections.h3: One stage, repeated stages and efficiency

blocks.text: L = rI;  M = A<sub>F</sub> + W<sub>F</sub> + S;  y = (A<sub>F</sub> + A<sub>S</sub>)/M;  V = M − L
blocks.where: I is kg inert solid; r is kg solution retained per kg inert; L is kg of solution in the underflow; A<sub>F</sub> is kg solute in the feed and W<sub>F</sub> kg solvent (liquid) already in it; S is kg of fresh solvent stream and A<sub>S</sub> the solute it brings (0 if pure); M is the total solution; y its solute mass fraction, valid while all solute dissolves and the solution is below saturation; V is kg of overflow.

blocks.text: Solute in the overflow is Vy and in the underflow Ly. Recovery of the solid's solute is (Vy − A<sub>S</sub>)/A<sub>F</sub>. If the solvent is too little to dissolve all the solute, y is the saturation value and the undissolved solute leaves with the underflow as solid.

Multistage cross-current leaching: the underflow from stage 1 (I kg inert with L kg solution at y1) is mixed with a fresh portion of solvent in stage 2, and so on. With constant r and pure solvent portions W, each later stage keeps yn = yn−1L/(L + W). Every stage needs fresh solvent and every overflow is weaker, so the combined product is dilute; counter-current washing, in the last chapter of this unit, is the usual plant route.

Stage efficiency: a real stage dissolves less solute than an ideal one when the contact time is short or the particles are thick. It is defined on the solute leached: η = (solute actually leached)/(solute leached in an ideal stage). The overall efficiency, ideal stages divided by real stages, is used to turn a stage count into equipment.

items: Agitated vessels: a stirred tank for fine solids; the slurry is then filtered or settled. The Pachuca tank, a tall cone-bottomed tank stirred by compressed air rising in a central tube, handles fine ore slurries with no moving parts in the liquid.
Fixed-bed (percolation) extractors for coarse solids: solvent percolates through a stationary bed of coffee, tea, herbs or sugar-beet cossettes; batteries of these form the Shanks system.

Thickeners: a Dorr thickener is a wide shallow tank with a slow rake; clear overflow leaves at the rim and thick underflow is drawn from the centre. A row of thickeners with solids going one way and wash liquor the other is continuous counter-current decantation (CCD), used for ores and alumina.

Moving-bed extractors for flakes and seeds: the Bollman extractor carries perforated baskets on a bucket elevator, with solvent sprayed on them; the Rotocel turns a ring of baskets under solvent sprays; the Kennedy extractor pushes solids through a row of tubs with paddles while solvent flows the other way; screw-conveyor extractors (the Hildebrandt type) move the solid up a U-shaped screw against the solvent.

examples.question: 1000 kg of seeds holding 20 mass% oil and 80 mass% inert meal is leached in one ideal stage with 500 kg of pure solvent. The underflow retains 0.5 kg of solution per kg of inert. Find the oil in the overflow and the recovery.
steps: Inert I = 0.80 × 1000 = 800 kg; oil A<sub>F</sub> = 200 kg; no liquid in the feed.
All the oil dissolves: total solution M = 200 + 500 = 700 kg, y = 200/700 = 0.2857 kg oil per kg solution.
Overflow V = M − L = 700 − 400 = 300 kg, carrying 300 × 0.2857 = 85.7 kg oil.
Underflow: 800 kg inert + 400 kg solution with 400 × 0.2857 = 114.3 kg oil. Check: 85.7 + 114.3 = 200 kg.
examples.answer: The overflow carries 85.7 kg of oil (42.9 % recovery); 114.3 kg stays in the wet meal.

examples.question: The underflow of the first example is leached again in a second ideal cross-current stage with another 500 kg of pure solvent. Find the total recovery. What would the same 500 kg have given if split into two portions of 250 kg?
steps: Stage 2 input: 800 kg inert with 400 kg solution holding 114.3 kg oil, plus 500 kg solvent. M<sub>2</sub> = 900 kg, y<sub>2</sub> = 114.3/900 = 0.1270.
V<sub>2</sub> = 900 − 400 = 500 kg carrying 63.5 kg oil; underflow keeps 400 × 0.1270 = 50.8 kg.
Total recovered = 85.7 + 63.5 = 149.2 kg, recovery 74.6 % for 1000 kg of solvent.

Split 250 + 250: stage 1 M = 450 kg, y<sub>1</sub> = 0.4444, V<sub>1</sub> = 50 kg with 22.2 kg oil; stage 2 has 177.8 kg oil in 650 kg, y<sub>2</sub> = 0.2735, V<sub>2</sub> = 250 kg with 68.4 kg oil.
Recovery with the split = (22.2 + 68.4)/200 = 45.3 %, only a little above 42.9 %: when the underflow holds 400 kg of the solution, small portions are mostly soaked up by it.
examples.answer: Two stages of 500 kg recover 74.6 %; the same 500 kg split in two recovers 45.3 %.

traps: Write the balances on the inert solid, not on the total solid: the solid loses mass as the solute dissolves, the inert does not.
The underflow is wet: the overflow is M − rI, not the whole solvent charged (300 kg, not 500 kg, in the first example).
r must be kg solution per kg inert; if the data give kg solution per kg of underflow or kg solvent per kg inert, convert first.
The ideal-stage formula y = A<sub>F</sub>/M assumes all the solute dissolves; if y comes out above the solubility, the solution is saturated and some solute stays undissolved.
Recovery counts only solute that came from the solid; solute brought in with an impure solvent is subtracted.

quiz.q: Define overflow and underflow in leaching.
quiz.a: Overflow is the clear solution free of inert solid. Underflow is the inert solid together with the solution it retains.
The Bollman (basket) extractor and the Rotocel; also the Kennedy and screw-conveyor extractors.

quiz.q: Why are leaching balances written on the inert solid?
quiz.a: The inert mass is the same in every stream and stage, while the total solid changes as solute dissolves; the retained solution is also stated per kg inert, so r and L stay well defined.

quiz.q: What does a vertical tie line on the N–y diagram mean?
quiz.a: The overflow and the solution in the underflow have the same composition: an ideal stage with all the solute dissolved and no adsorption on the solid.

quiz.q: Spent solid contains 800 kg inert and retains r = 0.45 kg solution per kg inert. How much solution leaves with it?
One ideal stage: 100 kg solute in a dry feed, 400 kg pure solvent, rI = 200 kg. Find y and the solute in the overflow.
quiz.a: M = 500 kg, y = 0.2; V = 300 kg with 60 kg solute; recovery 60 %.

quiz.q: In one stage more solvent raises recovery but weakens the overflow. Show this with the first example using 1000 kg of solvent.
quiz.a: M = 1200 kg, y = 0.1667; V = 800 kg with 133.3 kg oil: recovery 66.7 % against 42.9 %, but the overflow is 0.167 instead of 0.286 kg/kg, so more solvent must be evaporated per kg of oil.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real retention r depends on particle size, drainage time and solution viscosity, so plants measure a retention curve and draw a curved underflow line. Gold and copper heap leaching treats millions of tonnes of crushed ore on lined pads, irrigated for months. Ultrasound, microwave and pressurised hot-water extraction speed up the diffusion step for herbal products. Search for counter-current decantation, heap leaching and Rotocel extractor.

figure.caption: The worked examples: in each ideal stage all the oil is dissolved, the overflow and the retained solution leave at the same strength, and the meal always carries 400 kg of solution forward. One stage recovers 85.7 kg of the 200 kg of oil; a second stage with fresh solvent adds 63.5 kg.
